awd_titl_txt: RAPID: Water Concentrations and Emissions of Sewage-Related Compounds for the Tijuana River--Air Quality Effects for San Diego County, California
awd_abstract_narration:
This RAPID project will investigate high ambient air levels of hydrogen sulfide in south San Diego County associated with the ongoing discharge of untreated municipal and industrial sewage to the Tijuana River. There are health concerns caused by breathing in fumes of hydrogen sulfide, as well as concerns about adverse health effects from the particulate sulfate that can be formed from the oxidation of hydrogen sulfide. It is important to measure the concentration of these toxic compounds in the river water and determine the related amounts in the air during wintertime periods of low precipitation before the spring rains dilute their concentrations. This work will address important issues regarding the emissions of acutely and chronically harmful substances being discharged into the river and subsequently released into the atmosphere.

This project focuses on time and location dependent water-phase concentration data and modeling of the air-to-water emissions of important volatilizable compounds from the Tijuana River system. This data will be used with other information needed for estimating overall air-liquid mass transfer coefficients based on (a) the liquid-side resistance values (as determined primarily by flow velocity and depth regimes); and (b) the air-side resistance (as determined primarily by wind velocity regimes). The relative magnitudes of the two resistances are affected by the compound itself and temperature-dependent Henry’s Gas Law Constant.  Researchers from the University of California at San Diego and the University of California at Riverside will collaborate on efforts that use river water concentration data with temperature-dependent Henry’s Gas Law Constant values, flow rate and depth data/estimates, and meteorological wind data to estimate temporally dependent emissions from the Tijuana River system to the San Diego/Tijuana air shed for use in air quality modeling. The knowledge gained from this work will inform the understanding of the air quality affecting populations at widely different scales, ranging from those who live and work in the local area, to the region surrounding and including the city of San Diego, and ultimately to the entire area affected by the transport of these emissions into other regions of the country.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report for the General Public (POR) – 10/01/2026

Federal Award ID Number: 2525496

Project Title:  RAPID: Water Concentrations and Emissions of Sewage-Related Compounds for the Tijuana River

PI: James F. Pankow

Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Portland State University, Portland, Oregon, 97207

 

Abstract at the Time of Award

 A project is proposed to complement on-going research by Dr. Kim Prather (UCSD) on air emis-sions from the Tijuana River to the San Diego, CA airshed.  Only a funded RAPID proposal would enable immediate reciprocal leveraging of the work by Dr. Prather.  Emitted compounds of concern include H2S which is present in local air at levels of concern for reasons of both acute toxicity and regional sulfur emissions.  Other volatile sulfur-containing compounds are certainly being emitted, along with volatile compounds problematic for regional air pollution due to SOA PM and ozone formation.  Sampling will take place in collaboration with UCSD, with subsequent analyses at PSU using an array of advanced analytical methods and targeting multiple analytes of concern.  The analytes will also include the biological oxygen demand, which will be used as a measure of likely continued H2S production in, and emission from, the river/estuary system.  The data obtained will be of critical utility for water-to-air volatilization modeling, which will be carried out in collaboration with Dr. Porter (UCR).  Analytical screening at PSU will also take place for non-volatile industrial emerging contaminant compounds such as the forever chemical PFAS class, and pharmaceuticals, which may be aerosolized from the contaminated river at points of discharge and diversion/ channeling via culverts.   

Publications Produced as a Result of this Research

None as of 10/01/2026 (work on publications is underway).

Project Outcomes

The goals of this project were to bring online and immediately apply the analytical methods needed for measuring the concentrations in the sewage-contaminated Tijuana River of numerous parameters of interest including: 1) hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and other problematic sulfur-containing compounds; 2) various nitrogen-containing compounds such as odiferous amines, including several methyl amines; 3) industrial chemical solvents as from machining operations; and 4) salt ions such sodium and chloride as indicators of industrial discharges.  The utilized advanced analytical methods included gas chromatography with mass spectrometry (GC/MS) for the organic pollutants such as the organic sulfur- and nitrogen-containing compounds and the VOCs, and ion chromatography (IC) for the ions. 

All needed analytical methods were successfully developed.  Multiple rounds of samplings in the river were successfully carried by the UCSD team and the samples sent to and analyzed by the PSU team.  A summary of results for sampling on August 13, 2025 is given in Table 1.
